title: Cloud Providers & AWS Fundamentals
summary: Cloud providers — AWS, GCP, Azure — are the infrastructure layer under every modern DevOps stack. AWS is the market leader. Understanding compute (EC2), storage (S3), networking (VPC, IAM), and managed Kubernetes (EKS) gives you a foundation that translates across all three clouds.

sections.title: Cloud computing models: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS
sections.body:
Cloud providers rent you infrastructure on demand. You pay for what you use and scale in seconds instead of ordering servers.

**Service models:**

```
On-Premises  →  You manage everything (hardware, OS, runtime, app)
IaaS         →  Provider manages hardware; you manage OS up
PaaS         →  Provider manages OS + runtime; you manage app
SaaS         →  Provider manages everything; you use the software

Examples:
  IaaS:  AWS EC2, GCP Compute Engine, Azure VMs
  PaaS:  Heroku, AWS Elastic Beanstalk, Google App Engine
  SaaS:  GitHub, Datadog, Slack
```

**Deployment models:**

```
Public cloud   — infrastructure owned by provider, shared with others
               (AWS, GCP, Azure)

Private cloud  — infrastructure dedicated to one org
               (on-prem VMware, OpenStack)

Hybrid cloud   — mix of public and private
               (data on-prem, compute in cloud)

Multi-cloud    — using multiple public providers
               (AWS for compute, GCP for ML, Azure for M365 integration)
```

**Core cloud concepts:**

```
Region         — geographic area with multiple data centers
               (us-east-1, eu-west-1, ap-southeast-1)

Availability Zone (AZ) — isolated data center within a region
               (us-east-1a, us-east-1b, us-east-1c)
               Spread resources across AZs for high availability

Edge Location  — CDN endpoint, closer to users
               (CloudFront for AWS)

VPC            — Virtual Private Cloud: your isolated network

IAM            — Identity and Access Management: who can do what

Managed Service — provider runs the infrastructure component
               (RDS = managed Postgres, ElastiCache = managed Redis)
```

**Why cloud over on-prem?**
- No upfront hardware cost (OpEx vs CapEx)
- Horizontal scaling in seconds (autoscaling)
- Global availability without building data centers
- Managed services eliminate undifferentiated heavy lifting
- Pay-per-use: idle resources cost nothing if you terminate them

sections.title: IAM: identity, users, roles, and policies
sections.body:
AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) controls who can do what in your AWS account. Getting IAM right is the foundation of cloud security.

**Core IAM objects:**

```
User         — a person or service with long-term credentials
               (avoid for applications — use roles instead)

Group        — collection of users sharing the same policies
               (Developers, Ops, ReadOnly)

Role         — a set of permissions that can be assumed
               (an EC2 instance assumes a role to call S3)
               No static credentials — uses temporary tokens

Policy       — JSON document defining allowed/denied actions
               Attached to users, groups, or roles
```

**Policy document anatomy:**

```json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "AllowS3ReadOnlyForBucket",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "s3:GetObject",
        "s3:ListBucket"
      ],
      "Resource": [
        "arn:aws:s3:::my-app-bucket",
        "arn:aws:s3:::my-app-bucket/*"
      ]
    },
    {
      "Sid": "DenyDeleteAnywhere",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": "s3:DeleteObject",
      "Resource": "*"
    }
  ]
}
```

**IAM best practices:**

```
✗ Root account for daily use         → use it only for billing
✗ Long-term credentials for apps     → use IAM roles
✗ Wildcard actions (s3:*)            → scope to specific actions
✗ Sharing credentials                → one IAM user per person

✓ Enable MFA on root + all users
✓ Principle of least privilege: grant only what's needed
✓ Use IAM roles for EC2/Lambda/EKS
✓ Rotate access keys regularly
✓ Use AWS Organizations for multi-account structure
```

**Assume role (how apps get temporary credentials):**

```bash
# AWS CLI: assume a role and get temporary credentials
aws sts assume-role \
  --role-arn arn:aws:iam::123456789:role/deploy-role \
  --role-session-name ci-deploy

# Output: AccessKeyId, SecretAccessKey, SessionToken (expire in 1h)

# In Kubernetes (IRSA: IAM Roles for Service Accounts)
# Pods in EKS can assume roles without static credentials
# annotation on ServiceAccount:
#   eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn: arn:aws:iam::123456789:role/my-role
```

**ARN format:**

```
arn:partition:service:region:account-id:resource
arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket              (no region/account for global services)
arn:aws:iam::123456789:role/admin   (no region for IAM)
arn:aws:ec2:us-east-1:123456789:instance/i-abc123
```

sections.title: Compute (EC2) and storage (S3, EBS)
sections.body:
EC2 and S3 are the two most fundamental AWS services. Everything else builds on top of them.

## EC2: Elastic Compute Cloud

EC2 provides virtual machines (instances). You choose instance type, OS (AMI), network, and storage.

```bash
# List running instances
aws ec2 describe-instances \
  --filters Name=instance-state-name,Values=running \
  --query 'Reservations[].Instances[].[InstanceId,InstanceType,PublicIpAddress,Tags[?Key==`Name`].Value|[0]]' \
  --output table

# Launch an instance
aws ec2 run-instances \
  --image-id ami-0c02fb55956c7d316 \
  --instance-type t3.micro \
  --key-name my-keypair \
  --security-group-ids sg-abc123 \
  --subnet-id subnet-abc123 \
  --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=instance,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=web-server}]'

# SSH into instance
ssh -i ~/.ssh/my-keypair.pem ec2-user@<public-ip>

# Stop/terminate
aws ec2 stop-instances --instance-ids i-abc123
aws ec2 terminate-instances --instance-ids i-abc123
```

**Instance types (naming convention):**

```
Family + Generation + Size

t3.micro    — burstable, cheapest, dev/test
t3.medium   — burstable, more memory
m6i.large   — general purpose, balanced
c6i.xlarge  — compute-optimized (web servers, batch)
r6i.2xlarge — memory-optimized (databases, caching)
g4dn.xlarge — GPU-optimized (ML inference)

Sizes: nano < micro < small < medium < large < xlarge < 2xlarge < ...
```

**EBS: Elastic Block Store** — persistent disk attached to EC2:

```bash
# Create a 50GB volume
aws ec2 create-volume \
  --availability-zone us-east-1a \
  --size 50 \
  --volume-type gp3

# Attach to an instance
aws ec2 attach-volume \
  --volume-id vol-abc123 \
  --instance-id i-abc123 \
  --device /dev/sdf

# Volume types:
# gp3 (SSD, general purpose) — default choice
# io2 (SSD, high IOPS)       — databases
# st1 (HDD, throughput)      — big data, sequential reads
# sc1 (HDD, cheapest)        — cold storage
```

## S3: Simple Storage Service

S3 is object storage — not a filesystem. Store any file as an object in a bucket. 99.999999999% durability.

```bash
# Create a bucket (must be globally unique)
aws s3 mb s3://my-app-artifacts-prod-2024

# Upload files
aws s3 cp build/app.tar.gz s3://my-app-artifacts-prod-2024/releases/v1.2.3/
aws s3 sync ./dist/ s3://my-static-site/  # sync directory

# List
aws s3 ls s3://my-app-artifacts-prod-2024/releases/

# Download
aws s3 cp s3://my-app-artifacts-prod-2024/releases/v1.2.3/app.tar.gz .

# Make object public (for static sites)
aws s3 website s3://my-static-site \
  --index-document index.html \
  --error-document error.html

# Presigned URL (temporary access without making public)
aws s3 presign s3://my-bucket/secret-file.pdf --expires-in 3600
```

**S3 storage classes (cost optimization):**

```
Standard         — frequently accessed, low latency
Intelligent-Tier — auto-moves between tiers based on access
Standard-IA      — infrequently accessed (lower cost, retrieval fee)
Glacier Instant  — archival, millisecond retrieval
Glacier Flexible — archival, minutes/hours retrieval, cheapest
```

sections.title: VPC: virtual private cloud and network design
sections.body:
A VPC is your isolated virtual network in AWS. Every resource (EC2, RDS, EKS) lives inside a VPC. Getting VPC design right is critical for security and connectivity.

```
VPC: 10.0.0.0/16  (65,536 IP addresses)
│
├── us-east-1a
│   ├── Public Subnet:  10.0.1.0/24   (internet-accessible)
│   │   └── NAT Gateway, Load Balancer, Bastion
│   └── Private Subnet: 10.0.11.0/24  (no direct internet)
│       └── EC2, RDS, EKS nodes
│
├── us-east-1b
│   ├── Public Subnet:  10.0.2.0/24
│   └── Private Subnet: 10.0.12.0/24
│
└── Internet Gateway (IGW) — connects public subnets to internet
```

**Key VPC components:**

```
Internet Gateway (IGW)  — allows public subnets to reach the internet
                          attach one IGW per VPC

NAT Gateway             — allows private subnets to initiate outbound
                          internet traffic (but not inbound)
                          sits in public subnet, used by private subnets

Route Table             — rules directing traffic (0.0.0.0/0 → IGW or NAT)

Security Group          — stateful firewall at instance level
                          allow inbound port 443 from 0.0.0.0/0

Network ACL (NACL)      — stateless firewall at subnet level
                          rarely configured manually

VPC Peering             — connect two VPCs (same or different accounts)

PrivateLink             — access AWS services without internet
                          (S3 VPC endpoint, no NAT Gateway needed)
```

**AWS CLI: inspect your VPC:**

```bash
# List VPCs
aws ec2 describe-vpcs --query 'Vpcs[*].[VpcId,CidrBlock,Tags[?Key==`Name`].Value|[0]]' --output table

# List subnets
aws ec2 describe-subnets \
  --query 'Subnets[*].[SubnetId,CidrBlock,AvailabilityZone,MapPublicIpOnLaunch]' \
  --output table

# List security groups and rules
aws ec2 describe-security-groups \
  --query 'SecurityGroups[*].[GroupId,GroupName,Description]' \
  --output table

# Check route tables
aws ec2 describe-route-tables \
  --query 'RouteTables[*].[RouteTableId,Routes[*].[DestinationCidrBlock,GatewayId]]' \
  --output table
```

**Security group vs NACL:**

```
                Security Group    Network ACL
Level           Instance          Subnet
State           Stateful          Stateless
Rules           Allow only        Allow + Deny
Evaluation      All rules         Numbered order
Default         Deny all in       Allow all
```

sections.title: EKS: Elastic Kubernetes Service
sections.body:
EKS is AWS's managed Kubernetes. The control plane (API server, etcd) is managed by AWS; you manage the worker nodes (or use Fargate for serverless nodes).

**EKS architecture:**

```
AWS Account
│
├── EKS Control Plane (managed by AWS — you pay ~$0.10/hour)
│   ├── API Server
│   ├── etcd
│   └── Controller Manager
│
└── Your VPC
    ├── Node Group (EC2 instances running kubelet)
    │   ├── Worker Node (t3.large) — AZ a
    │   ├── Worker Node (t3.large) — AZ b
    │   └── Worker Node (t3.large) — AZ c
    └── Fargate Profile (optional: serverless pods)
```

**Create and connect to an EKS cluster:**

```bash
# eksctl is the recommended tool (wraps CloudFormation)
export CLUSTER_NAME=my-cluster
export REGION=us-east-1

# Create cluster (takes ~15 minutes)
eksctl create cluster \
  --name $CLUSTER_NAME \
  --region $REGION \
  --nodegroup-name standard-workers \
  --node-type t3.medium \
  --nodes 3 \
  --nodes-min 1 \
  --nodes-max 5 \
  --managed    # use managed node group (AWS handles AMI updates)

# Update kubeconfig
aws eks update-kubeconfig --name $CLUSTER_NAME --region $REGION
kubectl get nodes  # now talking to EKS

# Node groups
eksctl get nodegroup --cluster $CLUSTER_NAME
exsctl scale nodegroup --cluster $CLUSTER_NAME \
  --name standard-workers --nodes 5
```

**IRSA: IAM Roles for Service Accounts**

Instead of giving EC2 nodes broad IAM permissions, IRSA lets individual pods assume specific IAM roles:

```bash
# Enable IRSA on the cluster
eksctl utils associate-iam-oidc-provider \
  --cluster $CLUSTER_NAME --approve

# Create a service account with an IAM role
eksctl create iamserviceaccount \
  --name s3-reader \
  --namespace production \
  --cluster $CLUSTER_NAME \
  --attach-policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess \
  --approve
```

```yaml
# Pod uses the service account — gets S3 access without hardcoded keys
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: data-processor
spec:
  serviceAccountName: s3-reader
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: myapp:v1
    env:
    - name: AWS_REGION
      value: us-east-1
    # AWS SDK will auto-assume the role via IRSA
```

**EKS add-ons (managed by AWS):**

```bash
# List available add-ons
aws eks describe-addon-versions --region $REGION \
  --query 'addons[*].addonName' --output table

# Common add-ons:
# vpc-cni         — AWS VPC networking for pods
# coredns         — cluster DNS
# kube-proxy      — service routing
# aws-ebs-csi-driver — EBS persistent volumes
# aws-load-balancer-controller — ALB Ingress

# Install AWS Load Balancer Controller
export ACCOUNT_ID=$(aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text)
eksctl create iamserviceaccount \
  --cluster $CLUSTER_NAME \
  --namespace kube-system \
  --name aws-load-balancer-controller \
  --attach-policy-arn arn:aws:iam::$ACCOUNT_ID:policy/AWSLoadBalancerControllerIAMPolicy \
  --approve

helm repo add eks https://aws.github.io/eks-charts
helm install aws-load-balancer-controller eks/aws-load-balancer-controller \
  -n kube-system \
  --set clusterName=$CLUSTER_NAME \
  --set serviceAccount.create=false \
  --set serviceAccount.name=aws-load-balancer-controller
```

sections.title: Exercise: explore AWS concepts with the AWS CLI
sections.body:
The sandbox doesn't have AWS credentials, but the concepts and CLI patterns below are exactly what you'll use with a real AWS account. Run these commands against a real account or study the expected output.

```bash
# ── Install/configure AWS CLI ──────────────────────────────────────────────
# Check if available in the sandbox terminal:
aws --version

# Configure with credentials (for real AWS accounts):
# aws configure
# → AWS Access Key ID:
# → AWS Secret Access Key:
# → Default region: us-east-1
# → Default output format: json

# ── Query patterns you'll use daily ───────────────────────────────────────

# 1. List running EC2 instances in table format
aws ec2 describe-instances \
  --filters Name=instance-state-name,Values=running \
  --query 'Reservations[].Instances[].[InstanceId,InstanceType,State.Name,PublicIpAddress]' \
  --output table

# 2. List S3 buckets and their sizes
aws s3 ls
aws s3 ls s3://my-bucket --recursive --human-readable --summarize

# 3. Check your identity
aws sts get-caller-identity

# 4. List IAM roles
aws iam list-roles \
  --query 'Roles[*].[RoleName,Arn,CreateDate]' \
  --output table

# 5. Get all resources with a specific tag
aws resourcegroupstaggingapi get-resources \
  --tag-filters Key=Environment,Values=production \
  --query 'ResourceTagMappingList[*].ResourceARN' \
  --output text

# ── Cost awareness ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Always tag resources and set billing alerts:
aws ce get-cost-and-usage \
  --time-period Start=2024-01-01,End=2024-01-31 \
  --granularity MONTHLY \
  --metrics 'UnblendedCost' \
  --query 'ResultsByTime[*].Total.UnblendedCost'

# ── Security audit: find open security groups ─────────────────────────────
aws ec2 describe-security-groups \
  --query 'SecurityGroups[?IpPermissions[?IpRanges[?CidrIp==`0.0.0.0/0`]]].[GroupId,GroupName,Description]' \
  --output table
# Any security group allowing 0.0.0.0/0 on sensitive ports needs review

# ── Kubernetes: what you'd do with a real EKS cluster ────────────────────
# aws eks update-kubeconfig --name my-cluster --region us-east-1
# kubectl get nodes
# kubectl get pods -A

# ── In the local sandbox: k3s acts like EKS ──────────────────────────────
# kubectl is already configured against the local k3s cluster
kubectl cluster-info
kubectl get nodes -o wide
kubectl get pods -A --sort-by=.metadata.namespace
```
